summary: Provides a security framework for MPLS and GMPLS networks, describing threats, defensive techniques, and mechanisms for detection and reporting. It stresses RSVP-TE and LDP security, as well as concerns between autonomous systems and providers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a safety guide for MPLS and GMPLS networks, which carry traffic with short labels instead of full addresses. It lists the dangers, the locks and alarms that can help, and what to check when two network providers connect.

subtitle: A catalogue of the ways MPLS and GMPLS networks can be attacked, and the defenses providers can choose from.

tldr.problem: Security advice for MPLS and GMPLS networks was scattered across many RFCs, and no single document covered it in a consistent way, especially for links between providers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a trusted-zone reference model, lists threats to the control plane, data plane and management plane, then describes defensive techniques, monitoring, and provider and inter-provider security requirements.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework, not a protocol. It does not require every network to apply every technique, and it deliberately leaves out analysis of specific technologies.

today: RFC 5920 is an Informational RFC of July 2010, and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the general security framework for MPLS and GMPLS, and other documents may point to it for general considerations.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
MPLS and GMPLS are described in RFC 3031 and RFC 3945. Each of the many RFCs on them addresses its own security points, but no single document covered general security considerations. RFC 5920 fills that gap, and other documents may point to it for general considerations.

It covers threats, defensive techniques, and detection and reporting of attacks. It considers problems from malicious or incorrect behavior of users and other parties, and from negligent or incorrect behavior of providers. It then discusses service provider security requirements, with special emphasis on inter-AS and inter-provider links because the risk is higher there.

It limits itself to the provider's side and does not cover the connected user sites. It does not try to cover all current and future MPLS and GMPLS technologies, nor to define the precise mechanisms that must be implemented to satisfy each security requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Many small rule books each had a few safety tips. This one gathers the tips into a single guide for people who run these networks.

sections.title: Trusted Zones and Neighbors
sections.content:
The reference model treats each MPLS/GMPLS core in a single domain as a trusted zone: the core of one autonomous system within one service provider. The main concern is breaches from outside the zone to inside it. A key requirement is that interconnecting with another provider, the Internet or end users must not compromise the zone's security.

Neighbors can be authorized or unauthorized, and trusted or untrusted. An authorized neighbor is one you set up a peering relationship with, but it may still be untrusted. For inter-AS LSPs, the other provider is an untrusted but authorized neighbor, while customer edge devices are unauthorized neighbors. For inter-provider links the trusted zone of each provider ends at its autonomous system border routers (ASBRs).

Attacks unrelated to how the MPLS/GMPLS network is provisioned, such as general attacks from the Internet on a customer's web server, are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything inside one provider's core is treated as trusted. A neighboring provider may be allowed to connect through the gate, but you still do not trust it as much as your own network.

sections.title: Threats to the Network
sections.content:
A successful attack could mean observation, modification or deletion of data, replay, injection of inauthentic data, traffic pattern analysis, disruption of connectivity, degraded service, or probing of the network. Sources include other users of the same core, the provider's own staff, someone with physical access, social engineering, other providers, and the people who supply network equipment software. Attacks become easier as the shared infrastructure grows from one provider to many to the global Internet.

Control plane. Examples are LSP creation by an unauthorized element, interception of LSP messages, and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks on RSVP-TE (numerous unauthorized LSPs or a storm of RSVP messages) and on LDP (a storm of Hello messages or TCP SYN messages). Others are attacks through management interfaces and routing protocol attacks. Cross-connection of traffic between users, such as a site joined to the wrong VPN, is described as one of users' largest concerns.

Data plane. Examples are unauthorized observation, modification, spoofing and replay, deletion, traffic pattern analysis, resource exhaustion DoS and misconnection. In optical GMPLS networks, a misconnection may even activate unprotected lasers.

Management plane and insiders. Because of the chain of trust, the networks are particularly vulnerable to insiders, such as a malign person with access to any label switching router. The RFC says protection against insider attacks is largely for future study.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can try to trick the traffic controllers, flood them with fake messages, peek at the cargo, swap it, or send traffic to the wrong address. Sometimes the trouble comes from someone inside the provider.

sections.title: Authentication and Cryptographic Defenses
sections.content:
Devices should only accept connections or control messages from valid sources, and authentication should be bidirectional. The MPLS data plane is not amenable to source authentication because an MPLS label is only locally meaningful and the packet has no source identifier. The RFC also warns that cryptography does not protect against CPU or bandwidth exhaustion attacks, and software processing may even worsen them, though it can help against state exhaustion such as TCP SYN attacks.

Cryptography has costs: computation, configuration complexity, key management and larger packets. Where to apply it depends on trust. IPsec is called the security protocol of choice at the IP layer, and the RFC states that IPsec encryption without an integrity check is a state of sin. IKEv2 is the better choice over running IPsec without key management. Management traffic can be protected with SSH, SNMPv3 or TLS.

For pseudowires, the RFC lists specific weaknesses, for example that the PW label is the only identifier in the packet so there is no authenticatable source address, and that encapsulating PW packets in IP to use IPsec is not a valid option.

The RFC compares four places to protect traffic between sites on a path of CE, PE and P devices. CE-to-CE protects every link and resists compromised PE devices better, but gives the provider little visibility and scales as a mesh of customer sites. Combining access-link and PE-to-PE protection protects every link too, and lets the provider keep full enhanced services with a smaller mesh.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication proves who sent a message and encryption keeps its content private, but both cost processing time and effort. They do not by themselves stop a flood of traffic. The software needed to check authentication can make such a flood worse. A device should still accept only connections and control messages from valid sources.

sections.title: Access Control, Isolation and Monitoring
sections.content:
Beyond cryptography, the RFC describes filtering (one-direction packet matching, with actions such as discard, set class of service, count, rate limit, or forward and copy) and firewalls (which see both sides of a conversation and so can track state). Both have few options for encrypted traffic since only unencrypted fields are visible. Guidelines for DoS include ingress filtering everywhere, filtering attack packets at line speed, and not letting oneself amplify attacks. Management interfaces can be reachable only out of band.

Providers can use isolated infrastructure, such as a separate backbone or edge routers for VPN service, or aggregated infrastructure with per-service and per-user resource limits, including rate limits per VRF. Other defenses are operational processes that reduce misconfiguration, services that can be tested, and verification of connectivity along LSPs.

The RFC also recommends monitoring and reporting. Systems should collect information from PE, CE and P devices by SNMP or syslog, and flow information such as source and destination addresses, ports, class of service and TCP flags helps detect attacks. Reports should be batched so that monitoring traffic does not become a DoS itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Guards at the gate check who is allowed in. Some paths are kept completely separate, and sensors watch for odd behavior, but the sensors must not cause a traffic jam themselves.

sections.title: Provider and Inter-Provider Requirements
sections.content:
Section 7 lists protections inside one provider's core, for example anti-spoofing filters at the edges, authentication of control-plane protocols (LDP sessions may be authenticated with TCP MD5), and hiding infrastructure addresses. For RSVP-TE it covers isolation, neighbor filtering, message pacing, limits on control-plane resources, and RSVP message authentication (RFC 2747). LDP protection is similar, and the RFC says it is easier in a certain sense, since matching the LDP ports may be sufficient.

Section 8 covers links between providers, which the RFC calls high security risk areas. Equipment at the ASBR must be able to authenticate signaling sessions, supporting IPsec ESP with NULL encryption (manual keying is not to be used, and IKEv2 with pre-shared secrets or public keys should be used, with replay detection). It must rate limit and filter control traffic, limit routes learned from a BGP peer, enable protocols per interface with the default disabled, and detect cross-connection using LSP ping (RFC 4379). It also must verify that labels received across the interconnect were actually assigned to that neighbor, drop packets with unassigned labels, and limit the number of RSVP-TE LSPs and bandwidth reservations that another domain can create.

For MPLS VPN interconnection (RFC 4364), the RFC says inter-AS option a (VRF-to-VRF at the border) is commonly used, while option c is not normally used between providers due to higher security risks.
sections.plainLanguage: When two providers connect their networks, the border equipment must check every signaling session, limit how much traffic and how many routes can enter, and make sure the labels on incoming traffic are ones it handed out itself.

items.title: Control plane
items.text: Unauthorized LSPs, message interception, DoS storms against RSVP-TE and LDP, routing attacks.
